title: A mock election for governor, preceded by debates
body: The Herald announced a gubernatorial mock election on campus for the following Tuesday, to be preceded by debates. The result ran a week later: Western's voters gave Louie Nunn an easy victory over Henry Ward, matching the state result.
note: "Gubernatorial Mock Election Slated Tuesday After Debates" (47:7) and the result "WKU Voters Give Nunn Easy Victory Ward" (47:10) both check out. But no source ties the mock election to the student government, and the entry's date is the announcement issue: balloting was the following Tuesday, 31 October.

title: A presidential mock election on campus
body: The Herald announced campus mock election balloting for the following Monday and argued in an editorial that the vote would reveal how aware students were. The result appeared a week later: Richard Nixon and Marlow Cook carried Western.
note: "Campus Mock Election Balloting Set Monday" and the editorial "Mock Election to Reveal Awareness" are in 48:5. But balloting was Monday 21 October, not the 17th; the Nixon and Cook result is in an uncited issue; and no source ties the election to student government.

title: The Emme Kemp Jazz Trio opens the mini-concert season
body: The Herald of 31 August announced that the Kemp Trio had set a concert. The 1972 Talisman records the Emme Kemp Jazz Trio as the first of several small-scale concerts staged that autumn, the format the Associated Students adopted to give students better quality entertainment at lower cost.
note: Both halves of the sourcing are real — Herald 51:2 has "Kemp Trio Sets Concert" and the 1972 Talisman has "The Emme Kemp Jazz Trio presented the first of several small scale concerts staged during the fall semester" — but neither gives 2 September or any other date, so the entry's date is unsupported.

title: ASG launches a paper recycling project
body: ASG began a paper recycling programme, setting ecology trash cans at points across campus and later extending collection to cans and bottles. Money from the sale of recycled paper was ploughed back into the Environmental Committee's work, which was chaired by Joe Cheak.
note: The cited Herald 52:12, 6 Oct 1972 carries "Paper Recycling Project to be Launched by Associated Student Government" - an announcement of a future project, reported here as a completed launch. Every detail in the body (ecology trash cans, cans and bottles, money ploughed back, Joe Cheak) comes from the 1973 Talisman, which is not cited. Note also the cited issue is No. 12, not the unnumbered "6 Oct" label.

title: ASG books its fall entertainment fare
body: The Herald reported that ASG had booked its fall entertainment. The season it announced ran from the August bluegrass festival through the Doc Severinsen Homecoming concert, the America free concert and the Kiss date in December.
note: The headline is real - Herald Vol. 50 No. 2, 30 Aug 1974: "Associated Student Government Books Fall Entertainment Fare". But the body's description of what was announced is impossible: the 1975 Talisman states that ASG booked Al Stewart for 3 November, that Stewart's US tour was then cancelled over immigration law, and that only then did "LaCivita book Kiss... in the place of Al Stewart". Kiss cannot have been on a slate announced on 30 August 1974.

title: Linda Ronstadt makes ASG $4,300
body: Approximately 6,500 filled Diddle Arena for Linda Ronstadt on Saturday 1 November 1975, with Goose Creek Symphony and Andrew Gold on the bill. The Homecoming concert netted a profit of $4,300 for ASG, and Rick Kelley and president Steve Henry called it one of the most successful in years; its success guaranteed the free Spinners concert that January.
note: The cited Herald 51:19, 31 Oct 1975 is the pre-Homecoming issue; its only relevant item is "Linda Ronstadt Heads Concert Bill" - an advance notice that cannot contain a 1 November attendance figure or a profit. Everything is in the uncited 1976 Talisman: "Approximately 6,500 attended the concert on Saturday, Nov. 1. The Homecoming concert netted a profit of $4,300 for the ASG. Kelley and ASG President Steve Henry said the concert was one of the most successful in years. So successful, in fact, that it guaranteed another free concert (The Spinners and Wet Willie) on Jan. 30", with Goose Creek Symphony and Andrew Gold also named.

title: James Taylor closes the year with a free concert
body: James Taylor played a free concert on Friday 23 April 1976, with Henry Gross also on the bill. The Herald reported the following week that the James Taylor and Henry Gross concerts had been a big success.
note: The cited Herald 51:56, 20 Apr 1976 carries only "James Taylor to Play in Free Concert Friday", and 51:57 has "James Taylor Performance Will Be Tonight" - both advance notices. Neither names Henry Gross or ASG, and neither can support that the concert happened or the follow-up 'big success' report. The 1976 Talisman only says "James Taylor was scheduled to present a free concert in April."

title: Gerard O'Neill on space colonies
body: Gerard O'Neill, a physics professor at Princeton and author of "The High Frontier," told 100 people in the Center Theater that space colonies and orbiting solar power stations were possible with existing technology and could relieve the energy crisis. He said President Carter had abolished the NASA office exploring space colonisation while signing a bill to develop a particle beam weapon for use in space. ASG had signed him for $2,000 and the lecture was free.
note: The lecture content checks out but the money and the ASG attribution do not come from the cited source. Talisman 1979 Lectures section (p.97) confirms: O'Neill, Princeton physics professor, author of 'The High Frontier'; 'said in his April 2 lecture that space colonies and solar power stations are possible with current technology'; 'The 100 people in the Center Theater'; Carter 'had abolished a National Aeronautics and Space Administration office that was exploring space colonization'; Carter 'signed a bill for the development of a particle beam weapon... to be placed in space.' But the Lectures section names no sponsor and gives no fee - I read the whole section (Jarvis, Bethge, Goldberg, Koop, O'Neill) and ASG is never mentioned and no speaker fee appears anywhere. 'ASG had signed him for $2,000 and the lecture was free' is sourced from the 18 January 1979 Herald instead; cite that for the money.

title: The discount cards finally arrive
body: The ASG-endorsed discount cards reached campus, though the organisation still did not know how many it had or exactly what was on them. Distribution was held back while ASG worked out what the contracts, valid from 1 September 1981 to 1 September 1982, actually promised the merchants. Six businesses had been identified as buying space, though Steve Fuller thought at least fifteen had signed.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 57, No. 11, 1 October 1981

note: Herald 10-1-1981, Vol. 57 No. 11, 'Discount cards here, but won't go out yet' contradicts two claims. (1) The source says ASG 'still doesn't know HOW the 14,000 cards... WILL BE DISTRIBUTED' - the uncertainty is about distribution logistics, not the quantity or contents. The article states the count (14,000) and the contents plainly: 'The cards offer discounts to students from 21 listed merchants.' So 'did not know how many it had or exactly what was on them' misreads the sentence. (2) The reason distribution was held back is given as Bush being 'busy with other projects,' handing it to the communications committee, whose chairwoman Laura Simms 'is still working on a plan' - nothing about working out what the contracts promised merchants. (3) The 'six businesses... at least fifteen had signed' figures are not in this issue at all; they are in the 29 September issue (record 2412), and they sit oddly beside this issue's 21 listed merchants. What this issue does support: the cards 'have finally arrived,' were delivered the previous day, and were 'valid until Sept. 1, 1982.'

title: An ASG hotline opens on Wednesday afternoons
body: Student government established a hotline so students could phone in complaints and suggestions, staffed by the ASG secretary from 1 to 4 p.m. every Wednesday from 26 October on the office line, 745-4354. Anything the secretary could not answer was referred to an executive officer. Administrative vice president Adrian Smoot said students could already call any time but did not, and that setting a fixed hour made people more likely to ring.
note: Same article (Herald 64:17, 20 Oct 1988). The hotline facts are all correct: "Students can voice their opinions by calling the student government office at 745-4354 between 1 and 4 p.m. every Wednesday starting next Wednesday" (i.e. 26 Oct); "Student government's secretary will answer the hotline and take complaints and suggestions about the organization, Gott said. Any questions she can not answer will be referred to an executive officer." BUT THE QUOTE IS ATTRIBUTED TO THE WRONG OFFICER. The source reads: "Students can call anytime during the week, but they don't, GOTT said. But if a time is set, HE said 'people are more apt to call than just any day.'" That is Amos Gott, public relations vice president. Adrian Smoot, administrative vice president, is quoted elsewhere on the page - "We're doing well without one, but we could do better with one" - and that is about the vacant parliamentarian post, not the hotline. Verified on the page image. Reattribute to Gott and this entry is fine; note also that 26 Oct is a prospective start date in a 20 Oct paper.

title: Warren County judge-executive candidates come to congress
body: Administrative vice president Scott Sivley announced on 12 October 1993 that the Warren County judge-executive candidates, Miller and Buchanon, would be guests at the congress meeting of 26 October. The invitation was part of a run of outside speakers SGA brought before its own meetings that autumn, alongside Head Start and the state legislators questioned earlier in the term.
note: REJECT as dated - announcement only. SGA minutes, 12 Oct 1993: Administrative Vice-President Sivley "announced that Warren County Judge Executive Candidates Miller and Buchanon WILL BE guests at the October 26." There is no record here that they appeared. Separately, the entry's closing clause - "alongside Head Start and the state legislators questioned earlier in the term" - is unsupported: the Head Start speakers are in these minutes, but nothing about state legislators being questioned earlier in the term appears anywhere in this document. Cut that or cite it.

title: SGA moves to enter its own homecoming queen candidate
body: Congress voted in September 1994 to sponsor a candidate for homecoming queen, an idea the Herald put to a People Poll and drew an editorial cartoon about. The proposal set off a week of argument over whether student government belonged in a beauty pageant.

src.label: Herald 70:11, 22 Sep 1994 - Quarles, "Student Government Association to Enter Queen Candidate"

note: Headline verified: 'Quarles, Mitchell. Student Government Association to Enter Queen Candidate - Homecoming Queen', 22 Sep 1994. But the body's claim that the Herald 'put it to a People Poll and drew an editorial cartoon about' it is contradicted by the same issue: its People Poll is 'How Would Extended Alcohol Sales on Weekdays & Sunday Affect You?' and its editorial cartoon is 'Jimmy Carter Peace Delegation to Haiti'. 'A week of argument' is unsupported. Citation also mis-numbers the issue: the record is Vol. 70, No. 9, not 70:11.

title: Organizational Aid pays out $6,200 to 26 groups
body: Bill 98-9-F disbursed $6,200 to student organisations after two committee meetings totalling more than six hours. Awards ranged from $100 to the Residence Hall Association's $205, and reached groups from Free the Planet to the Jewish Student Organization.
note: The count is wrong. The bill lists 41 recipient organisations, not 26. Everything else checks out: '$6,200.00 budgeted for Organizational Aid'; 'over six hours in two different meetings'; Residence Hall Association $205 as the top award and $100 as the floor; Free the Planet and the Jewish Student Organization both present. Dated October 27, 1998.

title: First Dine with the Decision Makers
body: SGA held the first Dine with the Decision Makers on 8 December 2009 from 4:30 to 6 p.m. in the Cupola Room of Downing University Center, where students discussed higher education with elected officials over dinner. President Kevin Smiley said 25 students had signed up through an online RSVP, the number capped by cost, and that five legislators and Bowling Green Mayor Elaine Walker would attend. The event grew out of a decision by the Board of Student Body Presidents that autumn that Kentucky's public universities should each mount student lobbying events.
money: attendance was capped because of the cost of the dinner

src.label: College Heights Herald 85:24, 8 Dec 2009 - "SGA to dine with lawmakers" (TopSCHOLAR)

note: The cited article is a same-day PREVIEW, not a report of a completed event: 'Students have a chance to interact with legislators... tonight'; 'The dinner is set to take place from 4:30 p.m. to 6:00 p.m.'; 'five legislators will attend'; '25 students are signed up to attend.' The entry converts this into 'SGA held the first Dine with the Decision Makers on 8 December 2009', which the source does not state. The word 'first' appears nowhere in the article, and nothing establishes it was the inaugural edition. The individual details (Cupola Room, RSVP cap due to cost, Mayor Elaine Walker, Board of Student Body Presidents' autumn decision on lobbying events, President Kevin Smiley) are all accurate to the source; only the 'held / first' framing fails.
